title: Data & Machine-Learning Foundations
subtitle: From correct splitting and leakage detection to the right metric, data quality and drift
deliverable: Diagnose the data problem before touching the model: a sound split, a metric that matches the cost of error, and trustworthy data that can be monitored.
intro: This domain carries about 26 of the 150 questions, and its scenarios all share the same shape: “The model scored 98% in evaluation, then failed in production — why?”, “Which metric should the team report?”, “The data is imbalanced, leaks, or drifts — what is the first step?”. The rule the exam rewards never changes: diagnose the data problem before you touch the model. This unit builds the foundation the rest of the domain stands on: how to split data without leaking the future into training, how to read overfitting and underfitting, how to choose the metric by the cost of error rather than by habit, how to deal with imbalance, missing values and label noise, and how to tell real drift from a fault in the data pipeline. The next unit builds on this with the algorithm map, statistics, and metrics worked through with numbers.
outcomes: Choose the correct splitting method (stratified random, temporal, grouped, cross-validation) according to the nature of the data, and justify the choice.
Detect data leakage from its signals in the scenario and identify the correct first remedy.
Diagnose overfitting, underfitting and drift from the patterns in training, validation and production numbers, and propose the right remedy for each case.
Match the metric to the cost of error: recall, precision, F1, PR-AUC, calibration, RMSE, MAE and Macro-F1.
Apply imbalanced-data techniques in the correct order, moving the threshold before considering retraining.
Assess data quality across its eight dimensions, and design data contracts and validation at the ingestion, training and serving points.
Design labels and features: measure inter-annotator agreement, use active learning, apply standard transformations and know their traps, and respect the serving constraint.
method: Read every decision table as a condensed exam question: the first column is the “scenario cue”, and the remaining columns are the answer and its reason. After each section, cover the table and try to rebuild it from memory, then write yourself a short scenario in which the correct answer is counter-intuitive (for example: overall accuracy of 99.5%, yet the model is useless). Focus on the “first step”: the exam usually offers options that are all useful in theory, and the correct one is the cheapest that treats the root cause — removing the leaking feature before collecting more data, moving the threshold before retraining, and fixing the data pipeline before retraining on corrupted data.

sections.title: 1.1 The Correct Split for Each Situation

blocks.p: Before any metric, the split itself must be honest: the test set represents what the model will see in production, and carries no information that will be unavailable at prediction time. The splitting method is not a personal preference; it is derived from the structure of the data.

table: Independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) tabular data
Random train/validation/test split (for example 70/15/15), stratified if the classes are imbalanced
Preserves the class proportions in every part
Time series, fraud, demand, customer churn
Temporal split: train on the past, validate on a later period, and test on the most recent
A random split leaks the future, so scores are inflated
Group split: all rows of an entity fall in one part
Otherwise the model memorises the entity instead of learning the pattern
k-fold cross-validation (stratified / grouped / for time series)
A stable estimate that uses all the data
Tune on the validation set, and touch the test set once at the end
Reusing the test set repeatedly = overfitting to the test set itself

blocks.quote: The test set is touched once. Every tuning decision made while looking at it has made it part of the training.

sections.title: 1.2 Data Leakage: Definition and Warning Signs

blocks.p: **Data leakage** is information that is available at training time but will not be available at prediction time. A leaking model does not learn the problem; it learns the “answer” hidden in a feature or in the way the data was processed, so it looks excellent in evaluation and collapses in production.

blocks.h: Warning signs in the scenario text

ul: “Suspiciously high accuracy” or “excellent in evaluation, poor in production”.
A feature computed after the outcome occurs: for example **chargeback_flag** for predicting fraud, or **discharge_date** for predicting length of hospital stay.
Normalisation, imputation or feature selection carried out on the whole dataset before the split.
Duplicate records across training and test.
Target encoding without out-of-fold computation.

blocks.p: Note that half of these causes have nothing to do with the features themselves, but with the order of the steps: any processing that “learns” something from the data (a mean, a standard deviation, a list of selected features, the target mean per category) must learn it from the training fold alone.

sections.title: 1.3 The First Remedy for Leakage

ol: Remove the leaking feature (any feature that cannot be computed at prediction time).
Refit the preprocessing inside the training fold, preferably using a pipeline that guarantees this automatically.
Re-run the evaluation on a correctly split test set (temporally or by group where needed).

blocks.quote: The remedy for leakage is not “collect more data” and not “use a bigger model”. The extra data carries the same leakage, and the bigger model exploits it more.

blocks.p: In the exam, the tempting wrong options here are those that treat the symptom (poor performance in production) with a generic tool: more data, a different algorithm, or more regularisation. The correct answer always starts by fixing the split or the feature.

sections.title: 1.4 Bias and Variance: Overfitting and Underfitting

blocks.p: You read the state of the model by comparing three numbers: training performance, validation performance and production performance. Each pattern has a different diagnosis and remedy.

table: More data, augmentation, regularisation (L1/L2, dropout), a simpler model, early stopping
Richer features, a bigger model, longer training, less regularisation
Both high in evaluation, poor in production
Fix the split/features; compare training distributions with live data
Validation loss rises while training loss falls
Early stopping at the lowest validation loss

blocks.p: The third pattern is the most frequent in the exam, because it looks like overfitting but is not: overfitting shows up as a gap between training and validation, whereas here the validation itself is high, which means the validation set “knows” something production does not.

blocks.quote: A gap between training and validation = overfitting. No gap but a collapse in production = leakage or shift.

sections.title: 2.1 Choose the Metric by the Cost of Error

blocks.p: There is no metric that is “best” in absolute terms. The right question is: which error is more expensive — the false alarm (false positive) or the miss (false negative)? Do we need a decision at a threshold, a ranking, or probabilities that are used in pricing?

blocks.formula: F1 = 2PR / (P + R)        Fβ : β > 1 favours recall (e.g., F2)

table: “False alarms are costly/annoying”: spam, legal action, blocking accounts
PR-AUC beats ROC-AUC under heavy imbalance
Ranking quality independent of the threshold
AUC says nothing about the chosen threshold
Errors have a known monetary cost
It is the real business metric
Probabilities are used for decisions or pricing
Fixed with Platt scaling or isotonic calibration
MAE; and MAPE for percentages (beware of zeros)
MAE is in the target's own units
Macro-F1 (each class weighted equally) versus Weighted-F1

sections.title: 2.2 The Accuracy Paradox and the Two Meanings of “Precision”

blocks.p: **The accuracy paradox:** if the fraud rate is 0.5%, a model that always says “no fraud” achieves 99.5% accuracy and detects nothing. Therefore any option that cites accuracy on imbalanced data as evidence of success is a distractor.

**A note on wording:** the word “precision” in the exam usually means the classification metric TP/(TP+FP), not numerical precision (FP16/INT8), unless the scenario is about quantisation or GPU memory. Read the context before answering.

sections.title: 2.3 Threshold versus Model

blocks.p: A trained classifier outputs a score, and the threshold is what turns it into a decision. Many scenarios of the type “too many false alarms” or “we miss too many cases” are solved by moving the threshold along the precision–recall curve: this is the cheapest solution and needs no retraining.

ul: Too many false alarms → raise the threshold (precision rises and recall falls).
Too many misses → lower the threshold (recall rises and precision falls).
Retrain only if no threshold meets both requirements together, meaning the PR curve itself is low.

blocks.quote: Move the threshold first; retrain only when the curve itself cannot satisfy both requirements.

sections.title: 2.4 Imbalanced-Data Techniques

table: Tune it on validation, not on test
On the training fold only — never before the split (leakage)

blocks.p: Three traps recur: applying SMOTE before the split (so synthetic copies of test examples appear in training), forgetting that class weights distort the probabilities, which then need calibration and re-tuning of the threshold, and tuning the threshold on the test set.

sections.title: 2.5 Bank Fraud: The Full Exam Picture

blocks.p: Bank fraud is the scenario that brings together the concepts of this domain in a single question. Expect questions that combine two or three of the following six characteristics:

ol: **Highly imbalanced** — metrics: recall, PR-AUC, expected cost; not accuracy.
**Adversarial** — fraudsters adapt, so concept drift occurs; monitor and retrain periodically or when drift is detected.

**Latency-constrained** — the score must arrive before the transaction is approved (tens of milliseconds), so a lightweight model such as gradient-boosted trees is served in real time, with live aggregates such as “number of transactions in the last 10 minutes” drawn from the feature store.
**Delayed labels** — chargebacks arrive weeks later; monitor proxy metrics in the meantime.
**Regulated and explainable** — reason codes for declined transactions, and fairness across customer segments.

sections.title: 2.6 Evaluation Beyond a Single Number

table: Evaluation by slice (region, gender, age, channel, language/dialect)
Averages hide failures; this is the basis of fairness testing
A 0.5% improvement on 1,000 samples may be noise
From offline evaluation to the live (online) experiment
An offline metric ≠ a business outcome
Every new release must not regress on the critical cases
Automatic metrics (BLEU/ROUGE) correlate only weakly with quality
Read 50–100 errors before deciding what to change

blocks.p: The move from offline to live evaluation goes through deployment strategies (shadow, canary, A/B) that are covered in Unit 07. The point here is that a single number on a single test set is not enough for a launch decision.

sections.title: 3.1 Quality Problems and Their Preferred Treatments

table: Understand the cause (MCAR/MAR/MNAR); impute inside the pipeline; add a “was missing” indicator; deleting rows can introduce bias
Check first: an error or a genuinely rare event? (In fraud, the outlier is the signal); clip/transform; robust models
Log transform or Box-Cox; tree models are unaffected by scale
Audit a sample, measure inter-annotator agreement, write clear labelling guidelines, relabel the ambiguous slice
Remove duplicates before the split to prevent training/test contamination
Validate the schema, data contracts, lineage tracking; validate at ingestion (Great Expectations-style checks)
Minimise; use pseudonymisation; drop direct identifiers that are not needed (Personal Data Protection Law, PDPL)

sections.title: 3.2 The Feature Store and Training–Serving Skew

blocks.p: The **feature store** appears in training–serving skew scenarios: “The same feature is computed one way in the batch pipeline and another way in the real-time interface”. The problem here lies neither in the world nor in the model, but in the existence of two definitions of the feature.

ul: **One definition** of the feature, used by training and serving alike.
An **offline store** for training, with point-in-time correct joins that prevent leakage.
An **online store** for low-latency serving.

blocks.quote: Training–serving skew is fixed by fixing the pipeline (the feature store); retraining does not help.

sections.title: 3.3 The Data Lifecycle

blocks.p: Most machine-learning failures in production are data failures. A model is a compressed copy of the data it was trained on: if that data is late, incomplete, mislabelled or unrepresentative, no architecture will fix it. The expert engineer therefore treats data as a product with an owner, contracts, quality metrics and a lifecycle:

blocks.formula: collect → ingest → validate → store → prepare → label → version → train/serve → monitor → retain or destroy

blocks.p: As a sequence: collection → ingestion → validation → storage → preparation → labelling → versioning → use in training and serving → monitoring → retention or destruction. Each stage has its own failure modes and controls, and the exam often describes a symptom at one stage whose cause lies at an earlier stage (for example: performance drops at serving because a unit changed at the source during ingestion).

sections.title: 3.4 The Eight Data-Quality Dimensions

table: Impact on the model when violated
Audit samples against a trusted source
Required fields and records are present
Missing-value rates, record counts versus expected
The same fact is identical across systems
Available at the right time and recent enough
Stale features; real-time models running on old data
Conforms to type, format, range and rules
Parsing errors; outliers that are in fact faults
Covers the population the model will serve
Compare slice distributions with the target population
Poor performance and unfairness to under-represented groups
Cannot audit, reproduce or delete on request

blocks.p: When the scenario says “the model is weak for a particular region or group”, think representativeness; when it says “a request to delete a person's data” or “an audit”, think lineage.

sections.title: 3.5 Data Contracts and Validation at Three Points

blocks.p: When a source team changes a column's meaning, unit or type, every downstream model silently breaks. A **data contract** is an explicit, versioned agreement between producer and consumer that specifies: the schema, the semantics, the units, the allowed ranges, the freshness agreement, the owner, and the change process. The contract is enforced by automated validation at ingestion; violations stop the pipeline or divert the data to quarantine, instead of letting corrupted data reach training or serving.

blocks.quote: “The model degraded overnight after another team's release” → the permanent fix is a data contract plus validation, not retraining.

table: Schema, types, missing values, ranges, referential integrity
Distribution comparison against the last accepted training set, label distribution, duplicates, leakage checks
The same checks on live requests, with alerts

blocks.p: Tools from the Great Expectations, TFX Data Validation and Deequ family express these checks as declarative expectations stored in version control next to the pipeline.

sections.title: 3.6 Drift: What Changed?

table: A new customer segment, a new device type
PSI, KS test, Jensen–Shannon on the features
Verify; retrain if performance has dropped
A new fraud technique; purchasing behaviour after COVID
Retrain on recent data; train more frequently
The fraud rate doubles during holidays
Monitor the prediction rate and the label rate
A pipeline mismatch, not the world
Different preprocessing between online and offline
Compare the features logged at serving with the training features
Fix the pipeline (feature store) — retraining does not help
Currency changed from riyals to halalas; a field became empty
Fix the source; quarantine the corrupted data

ul: Before retraining, make sure the problem is real drift and not a fault in the data pipeline.
A sudden step-shaped change on a specific date → usually a source change or a serving skew.
Gradual degradation → drift.
With delayed labels, monitor input drift and the prediction distribution as an early warning.

blocks.p: Note also that input drift alone does not necessarily mean retraining: the response written in the table is “verify; retrain if performance has dropped”.

chapters.title: Labels, Features and Choosing the Model Family

sections.title: 4.1 The Four Label Sources

blocks.p: Supervised learning cannot exceed the quality of its labels. Labels come from four main sources, each with a different cost and noise level:

table: Domain experts or trained annotators following written guidelines
Highest quality if the guidelines are precise
Biased by the existing system (only what was shown gets clicked; repayment is known only for approved loans) and often delayed
Heuristic rules, keyword patterns and distant supervision from knowledge bases, combined through a label model
A model (including large language models) proposes labels that humans confirm or correct
Humans tend to accept the suggestion (automation bias), so auditing is required

sections.title: 4.2 Measuring Label Quality

blocks.p: Have several annotators label the same sample, and compute **inter-annotator agreement**: Cohen's kappa for two annotators, and Fleiss' kappa or Krippendorff's alpha for more than two. Kappa corrects for the agreement that occurs by chance.

table: An indication that the guidelines or the task definition need work

blocks.quote: Weak agreement is a specification problem before it is a modelling problem: if experts disagree, the model will not learn a consistent boundary.

sections.title: 4.3 Active Learning, Synthetic Data and Arabic Labelling Issues

blocks.p: **Active learning:** instead of labelling random samples, label the examples the current model is least confident about (uncertainty sampling), or the most diverse (coverage), or those on which the members of a committee of models disagree. This often reaches the same accuracy with a fraction of the labels — and it is the correct answer when “the labelling budget is the bottleneck”.

**Synthetic data:** generated records (simulation, generative models, text written by large language models) that help with rare classes, privacy-preserving sharing and testing. Its risks: it reproduces the biases of the generator, it may leak the generator's training data, and it makes evaluation optimistic if it enters the test set.

blocks.quote: Synthetic data may be added to training; evaluation, however, is done on held-out real data.

blocks.p: **Labelling issues specific to Arabic:** dialect variation (Gulf, Levantine, Egyptian, Maghrebi), code-switching with English, Arabizi (Arabic written in Latin letters), and diacritisation — all of them change what the annotator sees. The guidelines must state how to handle each, and the annotator pool must cover the dialects of the target users.

sections.title: 4.4 Feature Transformations and Their Traps

blocks.p: Features are the model's window on the world. In tabular problems, good features are often more important than choosing between strong algorithms. The following table lists the standard transformations and the trap each one hides — and the trap is what gets asked about.

table: Linear models, SVM, kNN, neural networks (scale-sensitive)
Fit the scaler on the training data only
The logarithm of zero or of negative values
Bins by quantiles or by domain
Non-linear effects for linear models; robustness
Loses information; bin boundaries from the training data only
Categories unseen at serving → an “other” bucket
In-fold target encoding leaks the label
Integer encoding that preserves the order
Do not use one-hot when order matters for linear models
Hour, day of week, month, holiday indicators (Ramadan, Eid, payday), time since an event, cyclical sin/cos
Time zones; Hijri versus Gregorian calendar
Counts, sums, averages over windows (last 10 minutes, 7 days, 90 days)
Windows must end before prediction time (point-in-time correctness)
Arabic normalisation and tokenisation must be identical in training and serving
Resolution and the colour-processing pipeline must match
Location can be a proxy for protected attributes
Division by zero; explosion in the number of features

sections.title: 4.5 Missing Values, Feature Selection and the Serving Constraint

table: The missingness is unrelated to any variable
Simple imputation inside the training fold
The missingness is explained by other observed variables
Imputation that depends on the other variables
The missingness depends on the value itself
High earners skip the income question
The missingness itself is information: add a “was missing” indicator

blocks.p: Simple imputers (median, most frequent) must be fitted inside the training fold. Model-based imputation (kNN, iterative) is more accurate but heavier. Boosted trees handle missing values natively.
Removes noisy or redundant inputs to reduce overfitting, latency and maintenance burden:

ul: **Filter methods:** correlation, mutual information, the chi-squared test.
**Wrapper methods:** recursive feature elimination (RFE).
**Embedded methods:** L1 regularisation, tree importance.
**Permutation importance** on the validation set is the most reliable general-purpose measure.
Highly correlated features share importance among themselves — removing one of them may change little.

blocks.p: A feature is valid only if it can be computed **at prediction time**, **within the latency budget**, and from data the system is **permitted to use**. A feature that needs a nightly batch job cannot drive a real-time decision within 50 milliseconds unless it is precomputed and stored in an online feature store. Features derived from personal data inherit the obligations of the Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL).

sections.title: 4.6 Choosing the Model Family, Baseline First

table: Structured tabular data, fewer than millions of rows
Boosted trees (XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost) — they usually outperform deep networks on tabular data
Logistic regression / small trees / boosted trees + SHAP reason codes
CNN or ViT, starting from a pretrained backbone (transfer learning)
Text classification with little labelled data
Fine-tune a small encoder (the BERT family and its Arabic variants) or few-shot prompting of a large language model; embeddings + logistic regression is a cheap, strong baseline
Boosted trees with lag features as the baseline; then specialised models
Transfer learning, active learning, weak supervision, LLM-assisted labelling with human review
Strict latency on an ordinary CPU
Linear models / boosted trees / small distilled models

blocks.quote: Baseline first. Complexity must justify its cost.

blocks.p: In a scenario where the team jumps straight to a huge deep model, the best answer is often: “Build a simple baseline and sound evaluation first.” The complex model is acceptable only when it beats the baseline by enough to be worth its cost in latency, operations and interpretability.

lab.purpose: Apply the “diagnose the data before the model” approach to a bank fraud model that achieved excellent results in evaluation and then disappointed in production.
scenario: A team at a Saudi bank built a card-fraud detection model on 12 months of data in which the fraud rate is 0.5%. The team split the data randomly 80/20, applied SMOTE and then normalisation to the whole dataset before the split, and used among the features the field “transaction was disputed”, which comes from the disputes system. The team reported overall accuracy of 99.6% and an AUC of 0.99.

After launch, the analytics team complained of many false alarms and, at the same time, large fraud cases were missed. Three weeks later, the model's scores suddenly dropped in a single day after the payments team changed the representation of the amount from riyals to halalas. Management asks for an ordered remediation plan with a reason for each step.
steps: Reject overall accuracy as evidence: with 0.5% fraud, a “never fraud” model achieves 99.5%. The right metrics: recall, PR-AUC and expected cost.

Detect the leakage: the dispute field becomes known weeks after the transaction, so it is unavailable at prediction time — remove it. SMOTE and normalisation before the split are additional leakage — move them inside a pipeline that is fitted on the training fold only.
Redo the split temporally: train on the older months, validate on the following ones, and test on the most recent; because fraud is time-dependent and adversarial.
Handle the imbalance in the cheap order: class weights first, then calibrate the probabilities, then tune the threshold on the validation set according to analyst capacity and the cost of a miss.
Handle the complaint about false alarms and misses by moving the threshold first; do not retrain unless no threshold satisfies both requirements together.

Diagnose the sudden drop: a step-shaped change on a specific date after another team's release = a source fault, not drift. Fix the source, quarantine the corrupted data, and add a data contract (unit: riyal) with automated validation at ingestion.

Add post-deployment monitoring: because labels are delayed, monitor input drift and the prediction distribution as an early warning, evaluate by slice, and keep reason codes for declined transactions.
traps: “Collect more data” or “use a deeper model” as a remedy for leakage — new data carries the same leakage.
Citing overall accuracy or ROC-AUC on highly imbalanced data instead of recall and PR-AUC.
Applying SMOTE, normalisation or feature selection before the split.
Retraining immediately on a sudden drop caused by a source change or by training–serving skew.
Tuning the threshold on the test set, or using the test set repeatedly during tuning.
A random split of temporal data, or of data with multiple rows per customer.
lab.deliverable: An ordered seven-step remediation plan that starts with the split and leakage, chooses the metric and threshold according to cost and capacity, and distinguishes a source fault from real drift.

review.q: A model achieved 97% on validation and 95% on test, then 70% in production. Is this overfitting?
review.a: No. Overfitting shows up as a gap between training and validation. High evaluation scores across the board with a production collapse point to leakage or distribution shift; the first step is to inspect the split and the features and to compare training distributions with live data.

review.q: Why is normalising the whole dataset before the split considered leakage?
review.a: Because the mean and standard deviation are computed with the test data's participation, so information about it leaks into training. The fix is to fit the preprocessing inside the training fold through a pipeline.

review.q: Hospital data with several visits per patient. Which split?
review.a: A group split by patient, so that all of a patient's visits fall in one part; otherwise the model memorises the patient instead of learning the pattern, and the scores are inflated.

review.q: The team complains of many false alarms. What is the cheapest fix?
review.a: Raise the threshold on the precision–recall curve without retraining. Retraining is needed only if no threshold meets the precision and recall requirements together.

review.q: When is PR-AUC better than ROC-AUC?
review.a: Under heavy imbalance; because ROC-AUC is affected by the large number of true negatives and so looks high. Neither says anything about the threshold chosen for operation.

review.q: A team used class weights, and the probabilities are used to price loans. What is the missing step?
review.a: Calibration: class weights inflate the probabilities, so they must be calibrated (Platt or isotonic), the Brier score and reliability curve monitored, and then the threshold re-tuned.

review.q: The model's performance suddenly dropped in a single day after the payments team's release. What is the diagnosis and the permanent fix?
review.a: A sudden step-shaped change on a specific date indicates a source fault, not drift. The fix: repair the source and quarantine the corrupted data; the permanent fix is a data contract with automated validation at ingestion, not retraining.

review.q: The same feature is computed one way in the batch pipeline and another way in the real-time interface. What is the fix?
review.a: This is training–serving skew; it is fixed with a single definition of the feature through a feature store (an offline store for training with point-in-time correct joins, and an online store for serving). Retraining does not help.

review.q: Cohen's kappa between two annotators is 0.35. What do you do before training?
review.a: The value is below 0.4, which indicates that the guidelines or the task definition need work. Fix the specification and relabel the ambiguous slice; the model will not learn a consistent boundary if the experts disagree.

review.q: Can synthetic data be used in the test set?
review.a: No. Synthetic data may be added to training, but it reproduces the generator's biases and makes evaluation optimistic; evaluation is done on held-out real data.

summary: You have mastered this unit when, facing any data scenario, you can name the correct first step and its reason: a split that matches the structure of the data (temporal, grouped, stratified), leakage removed inside a pipeline, overfitting diagnosed against leakage from the pattern of the numbers, a metric that reflects which error is more expensive, a threshold that is moved before any retraining, source faults and serving skew told apart from real drift, and then data managed as a product with contracts, validation, labels of measured quality, and features that can be computed at prediction time.
